instruction: none: started by the service for timer
headline: A timer run with no new instruction: it tested the plate check left untested last run and added two fixes behind it. The plate sinking is gone, and the two f* 0.3 stall layers get further: seed 2 from 6.22 to 6.59 and seed 1 from 5.88 to 5.91, out of 7.45 for the first cycle. No layer completes a cycle yet. Seed 1 now stops on a sphere resting against a side wall, which stacks do not treat as a contact. The f* 0.4 layer is limited by single stack integrations that take up to 112 seconds of CPU.

experiments.question: Does breaking a stack where one of its spheres without plate contact reaches the plate stop the plate penetration that ended the seed 1 layer, and let it complete the step to 5.90?
experiments.what_was_done: Ran the three stall layers (2D, 100 spheres, driving strength 2, depth 5; seed 1 and seed 2 at frequency 0.3, seed 1 at frequency 0.4) with the plate check, capped at 900 seconds of CPU each, and traced the seed 1 layer stack event by stack event from 5.85.
experiments.result: The check acted twice in seed 1, first on the very sphere that had sunk into the plate, and no layer stopped with penetration. But seed 1 then looped at one instant at 5.886: the sphere, handed back free while sitting on the plate, touched the rebuilt stack below it at the same instant, rejoined without a plate contact, and was cut off again at once. Seed 2 got stuck inside one stack integration in the step after 6.22 and was stopped by hand after 1307 seconds. The frequency 0.4 layer stopped at its cap at 5.27, as before.
experiments.takeaway: The plate check is right but incomplete: the sphere that reaches the plate has to land on it at that moment, not wait for the plate event behind other events at the same instant. The large slowdown seen with this check last run did not reproduce.

experiments.question: With that sphere landed on the plate at once and the pull rule applied at span restarts too, do the stall layers get past their last stops (seed 1 past 5.886 and to 5.89, the frequency 0.4 layer past 5.28)?
experiments.what_was_done: Same three layers with both changes, capped at 900 seconds each. Checked that each change acted by its own counter and by the first step where the run differs from the previous one. Traced the frequency 0.4 layer's slow step and the seed 1 stop.
experiments.result: Seed 2 passed 6.22 for the first time and reached 6.59 before its cap. There the pull rule was used fifteen times and the plate landing once, and the near-same-instant collisions of earlier runs fell from 19,779 to 4. Seed 1 differs from the previous run from the step to 5.87 and reached 5.91. It then looped at 5.918: one sphere rests against the right side wall, and every stack span through it is cut at its start because stacks treat the wall only as a boundary to stop at, not as a contact. The frequency 0.4 layer again stopped at 5.27. Single stack updates there took 18 and 112 seconds of CPU, so it is slow integration, not a loop. Largest energy gain at any touch: 1.2e-16, round-off.
experiments.takeaway: Falsified on the frequency 0.4 clause, but two of the three layers moved forward. The next two obstacles are clear: side walls must become contacts of a stack as the plate is, and the cost of integrating stacks of three to five spheres must be found and brought down. The plate landing ran only once, so it is lightly tested.

proposed_directions.direction: Make side walls contacts of a moving stack, like the plate (normal push and friction), so a sphere resting against a wall does not break its stack at every span.
proposed_directions.rationale: It is the current stop of seed 1 at 5.918 and will recur in any layer with spheres at the walls; it is the same kind of lasting contact the method is built for.

proposed_directions.direction: Instrument the stack integrator (steps, rejected steps, contact mode switches, force solves per call) on the frequency 0.4 join at 5.2508 that took 112 seconds.
proposed_directions.rationale: This cost decides whether the method can work without time-stepping, which is this line's closing condition; nothing else is known about it yet.

proposed_directions.direction: Make the CPU cap interrupt inside a long stack integration.
proposed_directions.rationale: Two runs this session and last overran their cap inside one call (one by 400 seconds), which costs CPU and leaves no result file.

unfinished_runs.reason: Seed 2 at frequency 0.3 got stuck inside one stack integration past its 900 s cap (the cap is only checked between calls); stopped by hand at 1307 s CPU, so it has a log but no result file. B0009 (open, affects L0018 and records no line) is listed as an open blocker.

run_conditions.limits_hit: none from the machine (load 7.4 on 40 cores at the start, 76 GB free, data folder 696 MB). The science was limited by the 900 s CPU caps chosen for the runs, so they ended inside the run's hour; local background jobs do not survive the run on this worker. uptime, ps, pmset, free, pkill and caffeinate are absent: load from /proc/loadavg, process CPU from /proc and the runs' own process_time, sleep could not be checked. CPU: E0108 2503 s, E0109 1949 s (from the runs), traces about 1200 s (from /proc and their logs; the first trace was killed early, the f* 0.4 trace stopped by hand), method tests 105 s, frozen tests 67 s. The first trace crashed in its own faulthandler watchdog (a tool fault, not the engine). Budget figure from program check (820.6) plus this run's 1.6. The E0108 and E0109 registrations were committed before their runs started (05:06:34 before 05:06:40; 05:18:56 before 05:18:57).
